title: Quonettquott
summary: Quonettquott is connected with the West Connecticut River, known as Connetquot Brook in Islip. The name is interpreted as at the long river.
why_this_matters: Preserved in early colonial land deeds, the Algonquian name Quonettquott translates to "at the long river" and still survives today as the Connetquot River in Islip. The endurance of such highly descriptive geographic markers demonstrates how Native languages permanently shaped the modern map and identity of Long Island.
history_content: The name appears in a 1690 East Hampton record naming Andrew Gibb of Quonettquott as attorney for John and Margaret Robinson. Dated source details are handled as a timeline entry.
translation_content:
Quonettquott is interpreted as at the long river, from elements meaning long, tidal river, and at.

Why Place Names Matter

“Toponyms are linguistic signs denoting a space and place and are tied to the way humans conceptualise and organise spaces.”

— Francesco Perono Cacciafoco and Francesco Cavallaro, Place Names: Approaches and Perspectives in Toponymy and Toponomastics (2023), Cambridge excerpt, PDF p. 2
preservation_content: Quonettquott keeps the Connetquot Brook landscape connected to older Long Island river names and to records that linked people across Suffolk, Queens, and East Hampton.
land_loss_content: Connetquot shows how Native river names shaped colonial land records and continued in modern geography. The same long-river term appears in multiple Long Island records, tying place-language to waterways, meadows, and deed boundaries.
whereintheworld_title: On This Site, Off This Site
whereintheworld_content: Quonettquott is associated broadly with the modern Connetquot River in Islip. The sources do not establish a surveyed historic boundary.
